## Opening question {.center}

A model looks at a photo and says: **"Cubism — 98% confident."**

. . .

It has never seen a painting. It has never heard the word *Cubism*.

. . .

So what did it actually learn?

## What models actually learn

Not concepts. Not meaning.

. . .

**Statistical patterns** in the examples they were shown —
edges, colors, textures, co-occurrences.

. . .

::: {.gold-box}
Your training data is your argument.
:::

## This is not hypothetical {.smaller}

- **Hiring tools** trained on past résumés (mostly men) learned to downrank women
- **Medical imaging** classifiers do worse on darker skin — trained on lighter-skinned datasets
- **Content moderation** misses harm in non-English text — the corpus was mostly English

. . .

Nobody programmed these biases. They came from **what was in the data**.

## Gender Shades

Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018 — tested commercial gender classifiers.

. . .

- Lighter-skinned men: ~1% error
- Darker-skinned women: up to **35%** error

. . .

Same code. Different faces. The gap was in the training set.

## Today {.smaller}

1. **Vocabulary** — 5 terms — 5 min
2. **Train** an intentionally biased model — 20 min
3. **Break it** on purpose — failure testing — 10 min
4. **Discuss** in groups — 15 min
5. **Pretrained models** — what's next session — 10 min
6. **Bridge** + exit ticket — 10 min

## Vocabulary {.smaller}

- **Training data** — the examples you show the model while it learns
- **Class** — one category the model sorts into
- **Confidence score** — how strongly it picks a class (0–100%) — *not* a measure of correctness
- **Overfitting** — memorizing the exact examples instead of the general idea
- **Bias** — a class systematically over- or under-represented in the data

# Hands-on {background-color="#003da5"}

Individual · 20 minutes

## Teachable Machine

A browser tool from Google. Trains a real neural network on **your** images — no code.

. . .

<teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/train> → **Image Project** → **Standard image model**

## Exercise — train a biased model {background-color="#ffb81c"}

*Individual · 20 min*

1. Pick **2 classes** with a hidden bias baked in —
   *e.g. "cat" but all orange vs. all black · "chair" but all office vs. all lawn*
2. Collect **10+ images per class** (Google Images, WikiArt — mind copyright)
3. **Train.** Then test with images that are *similar but not the same*.

**Record:** did it learn the category — or the color / background / lighting?

## Break it on purpose {.smaller}

| Feed it… | To find out… |
|---|---|
| an ambiguous image | where its decision boundary sits |
| something in **neither** class | whether it says "I don't know" *(it won't)* |
| a blurry / cropped version | if it learned the concept or memorized pixels |
| wrong subject, **same palette** | whether color or content drives the call |

. . .

Screenshot the confident failures. Those go in your Training Data Log.

## Discuss — groups of 2+

*15 min · pick someone to report back*

1. What did your model learn that you **didn't intend**?
2. How is this different from how a **person** learns a category?
3. Your model was never "unsure." What does that tell you about confidence scores?

## Confidence ≠ accuracy {.center}

A model always returns a number.

. . .

"92%" means *"this matches my training patterns strongly"* —
not *"I am probably right."*

. . .

It cannot tell you it wasn't taught enough.

## Transition {.center}

You just trained one model from scratch on ~20 images.

. . .

Next session: you borrow one trained on **1.2 million**.

## Pretrained models — a preview

**MobileNet** — recognizes 1,000 everyday object categories out of the box.

. . .

Trained on **ImageNet** — images scraped from the Western internet, early 2010s.

. . .

That origin is baked in. We'll watch it surface next session.
